title: Halfway There
statement: Let $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\}$, and let $h:S\to S$ be the function with $h(x)=1$ for $1\le x\le 4$ and $h(x)=5$ for $5\le x\le 8$. Find the number of functions $f:S\to S$ such that $f(f(x))=h(x)$ for every $x\in S$.
hints: The only values taken by $h$ are $1$ and $5$. Before counting anything, ask which values $f(1)$ and $f(5)$ can take.

Use substitution in the functional equation: write $f(f(f(x)))$ as $f$ applied to $f(f(x))$, and also as $f(f(\cdot))$ evaluated at $f(x)$. This shows that $f(h(x))=h(f(x))$, and putting $x=1$ and $x=5$ restricts $f(1)$ and $f(5)$.

The relation $f(h(x))=h(f(x))$ leaves two options: $f(1)=1,\ f(5)=5$ or $f(1)=5,\ f(5)=1$. It also shows that $f$ either preserves $\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $\{5,6,7,8\}$ or interchanges them. In each option, choose which elements go straight to $1$ or $5$; every other element must map to a chosen element. With $0^0=1$, the counts are $\left(\sum_{j}\binom{3}{j}j^{3-j}\right)^2$ and $\sum_{p,q}\binom{3}{p}\binom{3}{q}q^{3-p}p^{3-q}$, with all indices running from $0$ to $3$. It remains to evaluate them and combine the results.
solution: Put $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $B=\{5,6,7,8\}$, and let $f$ satisfy the condition. Then $f(f(f(x)))$ equals both $f(h(x))$ and $h(f(x))$, so $$f(h(x))=h(f(x))\quad\text{for all }x\in S.$$ Since $h(1)=1$ and $h(5)=5$, this gives $f(1)=h(f(1))$ and $f(5)=h(f(5))$, so $f(1)$ and $f(5)$ both lie in $\{1,5\}$. If $f(1)=1$, then $f(5)\ne 1$, since otherwise $f(f(5))=f(1)=1\ne 5$. Hence $f(5)=5$. If $f(1)=5$, then $f(5)=f(f(1))=h(1)=1$. These are the only two options. Case 1: $f(1)=1$ and $f(5)=5$. For $x\in A$, we have $h(f(x))=f(h(x))=f(1)=1$, so $f(x)\in A$. Similarly, $f(B)\subseteq B$, so the choices on $A$ and $B$ are independent. On $A$, let $J=\{x\in\{2,3,4\}:f(x)=1\}$ and $j=|J|$. If $x\in\{2,3,4\}\setminus J$, then $y=f(x)$ satisfies $y\ne 1$ and $f(y)=1$, so $y\in J$. Conversely, take any $J$ and send each of the other $3-j$ elements to any element of $J$. Then $f(f(x))=1$ for all $x\in A$: elements of $J\cup\{1\}$ reach $1$ and stay there, and the rest reach $J$ and then $1$. Reading $0^0=1$ for the empty map, $A$ admits $$\sum_{j=0}^{3}\binom{3}{j}j^{3-j}=0+3+6+1=10$$ choices. By the same argument, $B$ also admits $10$, so this case gives $10\cdot 10=100$ functions. Case 2: $f(1)=5$ and $f(5)=1$. For $x\in A$, we have $h(f(x))=f(1)=5$, so $f(x)\in B$. For $x\in B$, we have $h(f(x))=f(5)=1$, so $f(x)\in A$. Let $P=\{x\in\{2,3,4\}:f(x)=5\}$ and $Q=\{x\in\{6,7,8\}:f(x)=1\}$, with sizes $p$ and $q$. If $x\in\{2,3,4\}\setminus P$, then $y=f(x)\in B$ satisfies $y\ne 5$ and $f(y)=1$, so $y\in Q$. In the same way, if $x\in\{6,7,8\}\setminus Q$, then $f(x)\in P$. Conversely, take any $P$ and $Q$, any map from $\{2,3,4\}\setminus P$ into $Q$, and any map from $\{6,7,8\}\setminus Q$ into $P$. We check the condition on each part: If $x\in P\cup\{1\}$, then $f(f(x))=f(5)=1$. If $x\in\{2,3,4\}\setminus P$, then $f(x)\in Q$, so $f(f(x))=1$. If $x\in Q\cup\{5\}$, then $f(f(x))=f(1)=5$. If $x\in\{6,7,8\}\setminus Q$, then $f(x)\in P$, so $f(f(x))=5$. So every such choice is valid, and different choices give different functions. This case therefore contains $$\sum_{p=0}^{3}\sum_{q=0}^{3}\binom{3}{p}\binom{3}{q}\,q^{3-p}\,p^{3-q}\qquad(0^0=1)$$ functions. A term with $p=0$ vanishes unless $q=3$, because of the factor $p^{3-q}$. Likewise, a term with $q=0$ vanishes unless $p=3$. The remaining terms are: $(0,3)$ and $(3,0)$: $27$ each, total $54$. $(1,1)$: $9$. $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$: $36$ each, total $72$. $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$: $27$ each, total $54$. $(2,2)$: $36$. $(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$: $9$ each, total $18$. $(3,3)$: $1$. Their sum is $54+9+72+54+36+18+1=244$. The two cases are disjoint, so the number of functions is $100+244=344$. The answer is $344$. Why this works. functional-equation-substitution, casework, binomial-selection: substituting the equation into itself shows that $f$ commutes with $h$, which leaves two cases, each counted by choosing the elements that reach $1$ or $5$ in one step.
